lines.source: cold open over a night take-off drawn by the film
lines.text: This take-off never left the ground.

lines.source: 14 CFR Part 60, Appendix F, definition of a full flight simulator: a replica of a specific aircraft type's flight deck with a visual system and a motion cueing system; Level C and D require a six-degrees-of-freedom synergistic platform (Part 60 Table A1A/C1A item 5.c)
lines.text: It happened in here, inside a full-flight simulator: a copy of an airliner's cockpit, standing on six moving legs.

lines.source: EASA Part-FCL FCL.730.A (zero flight time type rating course; with a Level D FFS the pilot needs 500 hours or 100 route sectors on multi-pilot aeroplanes), AMC2 ORA.ATO.125(k) (take-off and landing training in the aeroplane except for courses approved for ZFTT); the first take-offs and landings are flown in line flying under the supervision of a type rating instructor (TS Form 2.23 ZFTT LIFUS, Danish CAA, 2026, quoting FCL.730.A). The U.S. equivalent: 14 CFR Part 121, Appendix H, Level C and D.
lines.text: The best ones are so realistic that, in Europe, an experienced pilot can learn a new airliner entirely inside one, and land the real aircraft for the first time on an airline flight, with an instructor beside them.

lines.source: framing of the film: fidelity (the senses) and timing (the transport delay limit), both proven by test
lines.text: How do you build a machine that pilots trust that much? It has to fool every sense, prove it, and never be late.

lines.source: Part 60 Appendix A, Attachment 1: general requirements grouped as flight deck, programming, motion, visual and sound systems; control forces are objective tests in Attachment 2
lines.text: Pilots don't fly with their eyes alone. They also feel the aircraft, through the inner ear, the hands and the seat. A simulator has to fool all of them at once.

lines.source: Part 60 Appendix C, Attachment 2, 18.a (visual display systems): on a non-collimated display the angle to a point depends on where the viewer sits
lines.text: Start with the eyes. On an ordinary screen, the two pilots would see the runway in slightly different places.

lines.source: Part 60 Appendix C, Attachment 2, 18.a: in a collimated display light rays from a given point are parallel, so the runway appears straight ahead to both crew members
lines.text: So the picture is reflected in a huge curved mirror. It sends the light out in parallel lines, as if from far away, and both pilots see the runway straight ahead.

lines.source: six-degrees-of-freedom platform (pitch, roll, yaw, heave, sway, surge) with a limited excursion
lines.text: Now the inner ear. Six legs can tilt and shift the cabin, but only a little. So how can you feel a take-off pushing you back into your seat?

lines.source: the otolith organs sense the gravito-inertial force and cannot separate tilt from linear acceleration; the equivalence principle of general relativity
lines.text: With a trick from physics. Your inner ear can't tell gravity from acceleration. Einstein noticed this too, and built general relativity on it.

lines.source: Part 60 Appendix A, Attachment 2 (motion system frequency response test): when simulating forward acceleration the simulator is accelerated momentarily forward for the onset cue and simultaneously tilted nose-up to generate a sustained specific force
lines.text: So the cabin slowly tilts back, too slowly to notice. Gravity pulls you into your seat, and it feels just like speeding up.

lines.source: the visual display is mounted on the moving cabin, so the scene stays level relative to the pilot; Part 60: the angular rates of the tilt do not occur in the aircraft and should be minimised; classical washout returns the platform to neutral below the perception thresholds
lines.text: The screen tilts with you, so the runway still looks level. Your eyes and your inner ear agree, and your brain is fooled.

lines.source: 14 CFR Part 60: full flight simulators are qualified at Levels A, B, C and D; EASA CS-FSTD(A) uses the same four levels; Part 60 Appendix A, Attachment 2: each objective test result is compared against validation data (flight test data) within stated tolerances; a driver program that runs the tests automatically is required for Level C and D
lines.text: Then it has to prove it. Simulators are graded from Level A up to Level D, the highest. To earn it, a simulator repeats maneuvers flown by the real aircraft on test flights, and its response must stay inside a narrow band around the real one.

lines.source: 14 CFR 60.19(a): the sponsor accomplishes all appropriate objective tests each year and completes a functional preflight check within the preceding 24 hours; transport delay is one of the objective tests (Part 60 Appendix A, Attachment 2, paragraph 15)
lines.text: The tests are repeated every year. And one of them is about time.

lines.source: Part 60 Table A2A, transport delay: 150 ms for Level C and D, measured from the control input through the host computer to the motion, instrument and visual response (Attachment 2, paragraph 15); a blink lasts roughly 100 to 400 ms
lines.text: When the pilot moves the controls, the simulator has a hundred and fifty milliseconds to answer. That's about the blink of an eye. Any slower, and it fails.

lines.source: old lab film, line 2: every stage spends the budget, image generation the largest share; the stages are the generic chain of a full-flight simulator
lines.text: In that blink, a chain of computers reads the controls, works out the flight, draws the world, and moves the cabin.

lines.source: EASA CS-FSTD Issue 1 (ED Decision 2026/008/R, Subpart D test 6.a.1, p. 467): 100 ms at fidelity level S for new devices
lines.text: Europe's newest rule cuts that to a hundred milliseconds for the most realistic new simulators. A chain that fit before can now be too slow.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 5 and 6: a fixed cadence (60 Hz), hour-long sessions; a four-hour session at 60 Hz is 4 x 3600 x 60 = 864,000 frames
lines.text: And it's not done once. It happens sixty times every second, for hours. A four-hour session is eight hundred and sixty-four thousand frames.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 7 to 9: E[K] = N p, so one frame in a thousand is 864 stutters a session; real overruns cluster
lines.text: If just one frame in a thousand is late, that's eight hundred and sixty-four jolts the pilot can feel.

lines.source: old lab film, lines 10 and 11: a rack of hosts publishes into one frame, which ends when the last host reports; old lab film, lines 13 and 14: one straggler makes the frame late; budgets are allocated and enforced per host, a system average constrains nobody
lines.text: Why would a frame be late? The work is shared by many computers, and each frame must wait for the slowest one. An average hides it, so every computer gets its own time limit, checked on every frame.

lines.source: old lab film, closing line, in plainer words
lines.text: That's determinism: the slowest frame counts, not the average.

lines.source: the author's view of why AI would enter a simulator: learned models of aircraft behaviour from flight data (system identification with neural networks; regimes such as stall and icing where physics-based models are hardest to validate) and neural rendering in the image generator; labelled as the author's view, no deployment claimed
lines.text: So why bring AI into a simulator at all? To make it even more real: a model of the aircraft learned from flight data, where physics is hard to write down, or a richer world drawn by a neural network.

lines.source: generative models and detectors take input-dependent time; any model shares compute, memory and scheduling with the rest of the host; a fixed-size network on dedicated hardware can be bounded, which is what the thesis asks for
lines.text: But now the AI sits inside the chain. Some models take longer on some inputs, and even a fixed one can stall when it shares a computer. One late answer, and the frame is late.

lines.source: the author's thesis, labelled as such on screen: two senses of determinism, repeatable outputs (a test is only evidence if the same input gives the same answer) and a bounded worst-case time
lines.text: So here is the thesis. AI can raise the fidelity that earns the trust, but only if it keeps the determinism that keeps it: the same answer for the same input, delivered on every frame, and proven, not averaged.

lines.source: closing line
lines.text: Fidelity earns the trust. Determinism keeps it.
